slide_1: MechEval is a code-graded benchmark that asks whether frontier models can solve real mechanical engineering problems, or only produce convincing physics errors. This walkthrough shows a live run: no recorded transcripts, no placeholders.
slide_2: Five tasks. A cantilever under point load and self-weight; a stepped axial bar; a statically indeterminate propped cantilever; thermal expansion acting against a clearance gap; and finite element mesh convergence with a stress singularity. Grading is deterministic: every required quantity is checked against a symbolic reference at one percent relative tolerance.
slide_3: The roster is four flash-class frontier models, called live through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint: GPT-6 Luna, DeepSeek 4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3 Flash and Claude Haiku 5.5. Each identifier is resolved and validated against the endpoint's own catalogue before a single token is spent, so a mistyped model can never be scored as a model failing.
slide_4: Here is the completed run for openai/gpt-6-luna. 15 trials, five tasks, three each. It passed 9 of 15, a pass rate of 60 percent. It solved 3 tasks on every attempt and failed every attempt at 2. Mean score 80.7 percent, mean latency 9.2 seconds, total recorded spend under one cent.
slide_5: The failures are the interesting part. On the indeterminate beam, deformation compatibility was never enforced: reactions were guessed as symmetric instead of solved. On the thermal task, a uniform three point six percent offset appeared across force, stress and expansion terms, which points at a rounded physical constant rather than a modelling error. Both are exactly the failure modes MechEval was built to catch.
slide_6: Everything here is reproducible in three commands: validate the roster, run the trials, generate the report from the run's own output files. The code, the transcripts and the graders are open source under MIT.
